title: Count Below Zero in a Sorted Grid
statement:
You get an m × n grid of integers. Every row reads non-increasing from left to right, and every column reads non-increasing from top to bottom.

Return how many cells hold a negative number. Zero is not negative.

examples.why: The negatives are -1, -2, -1 and -4. The two zeros do not count.

hints: Each row is sorted, so its negatives form one block on the right. How fast can you find where that block starts?
Binary search per row gives O(m log n). Can you reuse what you learned in one row for the next?
Because columns are sorted too, the first negative in each row moves left (or stays) as you go down. Walk a staircase from the top-right or bottom-left corner.

explain.intuition:
In each row the negatives are a suffix. Call c the column where row i's negatives start. Because columns are non-increasing too, the cell below (i, c) is also negative, so the next row's boundary is at c or further left. The boundary only ever moves left as you go down.

So start at the top-right corner. While the current cell is negative, step left; when it is not, every cell to its right in this row was negative, so add that count and step down to the next row. Each step moves left or down, so at most m + n steps.
steps: For each row from top to bottom: while col ≥ 0 and grid[row][col] < 0, move col left.
Now the negatives in this row are the columns col + 1 … n − 1; add n − 1 − col.
pitfalls: Counting zeros as negative by using ≤ 0.
Restarting col at the right edge for every row, which loses the staircase speed-up and is back to O(m · n) in the worst case.

solutions.title: Check every cell
solutions.idea: Count the negatives directly. It ignores the ordering, but is fine at this size.

solutions.title: Binary search in each row
solutions.idea: Find the first negative position of each row by binary search.

solutions.title: Staircase walk
solutions.idea: The first negative column only moves left going down, so one pointer sweeps all rows.

followups: Only the rows are sorted, not the columns. What is the best you can do?
Return the k-th smallest value in such a grid instead.
